column1: What fundamental optical phenomenon, documented by Ibn al-Haytham, underlies all camera image formation?
column2: Light traveling through a small aperture inverts and focuses an image on a surface (pinhole/camera obscura principle).

column1: Why is the projection of a 3D scene onto a 2D sensor plane described as 'lossy'?
column2: Depth information is collapsed into a single plane of focus; only objects at the focused distance remain sharp, while the rest fall into blur based on lens geometry and aperture.

column1: What is the 'exposure triangle' and what single physical constraint couples its three variables?
column2: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO — all three are coupled through the total amount of light energy reaching the sensor during an exposure.

column1: In the exposure equivalence principle, what stays constant across different aperture/shutter/ISO combinations that produce the 'same' exposure, and what changes?
column2: Overall image brightness stays the same; depth of field, motion blur rendering, noise texture, and dynamic range change qualitatively.

column1: What does 'one stop' of light represent mathematically?
column2: A doubling or halving of light energy — exposure values operate in a logarithmic (ratio-based) space.

column1: Why does raising ISO amplify noise rather than simply 'adding more light'?
column2: ISO doesn't capture more photons; it amplifies the existing sensor signal electronically, which also amplifies noise along with the signal — mathematically equivalent to more light but with a noise penalty.

column1: What perceptual/neurological reason explains why the rule of thirds is more effective than centering a subject?
column2: Human vision evolved to detect asymmetry and tension (dynamic equilibrium) rather than static symmetry; placing subjects near grid intersections (approximating the golden ratio ~1.618:1) engages reward circuitry (e.g., medial orbitofrontal cortex) and sustains viewer attention.

column1: What is the difference between magnocellular and parvocellular visual pathways in how a photograph is perceived?
column2: Magnocellular pathways register low spatial frequency information (overall shapes, tonal masses) first; parvocellular pathways deliver high spatial frequency detail (texture, fine edges) milliseconds later, creating a perceptual hierarchy.

column1: Why do leading lines effectively guide a viewer's eye through a photograph, per Hubel and Wiesel's research?
column2: The visual cortex contains neurons specialized to respond to oriented edges (vertical, horizontal, oblique); strong linear elements in a composition fire these line-sensitive neurons in sequence, directing eye movement along the line.

column1: What is the single invariant light-capture pipeline that governs all photography, regardless of artistic intent?
column2: Light enters the lens, is focused onto a light-sensitive surface (film emulsion or digital sensor), and is translated into a permanent record.

column1: What is the typical dynamic range of a modern digital camera sensor, and how is it measured?
column2: Approximately 12 to 14 stops, where each stop represents a doubling or halving of light energy.

column1: What does a histogram reveal about a photograph's exposure, and what do 'clipping' and 'crushing' refer to?
column2: The histogram maps tonal value distribution from black to white; clipping refers to blown-out highlights (lost detail at the bright end) and crushing refers to lost shadow detail at the dark end, both indicating exposure latitude has been exceeded.
